label: Opera Game 1858
game: Paul Morphy vs Duke Karl and Count Isouard

script.text: Paris, an opera house. Paul Morphy, playing White, faces two amateurs sharing the black pieces -- a Duke and a Count. They choose the Philidor Defense, a solid but passive setup. Sixteen moves later, Morphy has won. Here's why.

King's pawns come out, Morphy's knight jumps toward the centre, and Black props up with a modest pawn move -- passive, but sturdy. Then the bishop pins the knight. Morphy strikes in the centre, grabbing a pawn, and Black trades bishop for knight. White's already a touch more comfortable.

Now Black brings the knight to f six -- natural-looking, but it blocks the queen's defence of a key square. The queen belonged there instead; from f six she'd guard the loose pawn after White's queen swung to b three. Instead, that weakness lingers, and White stays comfortably the more active side.

Here's the moment. Black pushes a pawn to b five, trying to chase White's bishop away. But that's time spent on the wing while the king still sits in the centre, undeveloped and exposed.

Tucking the king to d eight was the stubborn choice -- ugly, yet it keeps the position breathing. Instead, White is now clearly better, and the pieces are already pointing at that stranded king.

And then the queen simply steps to b eight, offering herself with check. The knight must take -- but that's the point. The defender is pulled away, and the rook drops to d eight. Checkmate: the king, boxed in on its own back rank, has nowhere to go. Morphy wins.
Sixteen moves -- a miniature, chess slang for a game ended early. Morphy played at ninety-eight percent accuracy; his opponents, eighty-eight. The difference wasn't material. It was time.
